name: Escabeche
intro: One jar. Three weeks of acid and crunch.
card_uses: Spoon it over a rice bowl.
Stir it into beans, brine and all.
Eat it next to anything rich.
ingredients: 2 Anaheim chiles or 4 jalapeños, cut into rounds
1 cup white or apple cider vinegar
2 bay leaves, a pinch of dried oregano, a few peppercorns
method: Warm the oil in a saucepan over medium heat. Add the onion, carrot, garlic, and chiles and cook for about three minutes — just until the edges soften and the kitchen starts to smell like it. Add the vinegar, water, salt, sugar, and the bay, oregano, and peppercorns. Bring to a simmer, then take it off the heat immediately. Pour everything, brine included, into a jar. Cool on the counter, then refrigerate. It's good in an hour and better on day three. The ratio underneath this is the part worth keeping: one cup vinegar, one cup water, one tablespoon salt, one teaspoon sugar. That brine works on any crisp vegetable you have too much of.

storage.note: Keeps in the refrigerator for three weeks, and the brine outlasts the vegetables. Don't throw the brine out — it belongs on beans and in dressings.

uses.label: Rice bowl
uses.context: Add a little brine with it. Rice takes acid better than people expect.

uses.label: Tacos
uses.context: This is the jar that makes a home taco taste like it came from somewhere. Go heavier than feels right.

uses.label: Beans
uses.context: A spoonful of brine into a pot of beans does what a squeeze of vinegar does, with more going on.

uses.label: Chicken thighs
uses.context: Something crisp and sharp next to something rich and browned. That's the whole idea.

uses.label: A sandwich
uses.context: Chopped escabeche does the job of pickles, mustard, and hot sauce at once.
